READING

**Capacity arithmetic**

Four jigs at 41 tonnes each give a hard ceiling of 164 tonnes. Under MORVEDD, Thurlmere takes 96T and Marchgate currently takes 65T, filling 161 of the 164 available tonnes; Ostrey's 37 tonnes cannot fit, so releasing them is not a choice but a mathematical necessity. Under SALTGRAVE the book runs at 148T (the current level), leaving 16 tonnes of breathing room.

**Revenue comparison**

MORVEDD — Thurlmere: 96 × £15.40 = £1,478,400. Marchgate (assumed to hold): 65 × £14.19 = £922,350. Total ≈ £2,400,750/year, up roughly £301K on current turnover. Over the three-year Thurlmere term, assuming Marchgate does not move, that is approximately £7.2m, against a £96K capital outlay with a payback period of under four months of incremental margin.

SALTGRAVE — Marchgate: £922,350. Thurlmere retained at current volume (assumed): 46 × ~£14.19 ≈ £652,740. Ostrey on contract: 37 × £14.60 = £540,200. Total ≈ £2,115,290/year, roughly £285K/year less than MORVEDD. Over three years: approximately £6.35m with no capital out.

The revenue advantage of MORVEDD is real and substantial. It is not a close call on the income line.

**What MORVEDD actually requires Gallowfield to accept**

The uplift comes bundled with three structural conditions that interact badly with each other:

*Condition 1 — Single-point-of-failure concentration.* Thurlmere would represent 96 of the 161 tonnes being processed, roughly 62% of turnover. That is not merely a high customer-concentration ratio in the abstract; it is 62% sitting on a contract that can be terminated by either side on six months' notice following a change of control. The upside is capped at three years; the downside is uncapped.

*Condition 2 — The Vennerdale variable.* Thurlmere was acquired by Vennerdale in 2025, barely a year ago. Vennerdale is therefore an active acquirer, not a legacy family group. Active acquirers reorganise, sell subsidiaries, consolidate supply chains, and revisit procurement structures far more readily than independent mills that have traded with the same dyer for decades. The change-of-control clause — explicitly two-directional and activated by any further change of ownership — means that a second Vennerdale transaction, a portfolio disposal, or even an internal restructuring could hand either side a clean six-month exit. The fact that Thurlmere wants 96 tonnes (double its current volume) and dedicated infrastructure suggests Vennerdale is currently investing in this business line. That is reassuring. It is not the same as certainty over a three-year horizon under a parent whose corporate behaviour over the period 2025–2029 is unknown.

*Condition 3 — Ostrey must go, and go permanently.* A mill that has dyeing work placed with a partner for twenty-two years will not be easily recovered if that partner abruptly declines their three-year commitment offer, releases them, and then needs them back inside twelve months. Ostrey's offer of a three-year contract at £14.60/kg — better than the current average of £14.19 — expires 2026-11-28. Choosing MORVEDD means watching that offer lapse. It also means, in any scenario where Thurlmere exits early, Gallowfield faces its worst position with its most loyal partner already gone and no contractual right to reclaim that volume.

**Downside scenarios compared**

*MORVEDD worst case — Thurlmere triggers change-of-control exit after, say, twelve months.* Six months' notice means Gallowfield loses Thurlmere's 96T after month eighteen at the latest. What remains? Marchgate, 65T, at £14.19/kg, with no signed contract, generating £922,350/year. Ostrey is gone. The two dedicated jigs still belong to Gallowfield (the problem is clear on this), but they are infrastructure configured for a customer who is no longer there. The £96K spent on pumps and a separate liquor circuit is not lost capital, but it delivers no incremental value until a replacement customer of comparable size is found for that dedicated configuration. Capacity utilisation falls from 98% to under 40%. Revenue falls by roughly 60% from the peak. A 19-person business with £84K in remaining cash after the capex (before any bank draw) and a suddenly near-empty order book is in a difficult position.

*SALTGRAVE worst case — Thurlmere, having been declined, withdraws their existing 46T too.* This is the legitimate concern. A customer that wanted dedicated infrastructure and was told no may consolidate all its dyeing with whoever does take the contract. If Thurlmere leaves entirely under SALTGRAVE, the book becomes Marchgate (65T, £922,350) plus Ostrey on contract (37T, £540,200) = 102T, £1,462,550/year. That is a meaningful revenue drop but the business remains viable, has two customers, one contractually committed for three years, and has £180K cash intact and a bank facility untouched. It is a recoverable position.

The asymmetry matters: MORVEDD's worst case leaves Gallowfield with one contractually uncommitted customer, near-zero spare capacity to fill (since the other jigs are configured for Thurlmere), and no Ostrey. SALTGRAVE's worst case leaves Gallowfield with two customers, one contractually locked in, full cash reserves, and full operational flexibility.

**Marchgate's position under both courses**

Marchgate has signed nothing. Under MORVEDD, 38% of total revenue (65T × £14.19) remains entirely at-will. Combined with Thurlmere's change-of-control clause, this means both the largest and second-largest income streams carry no contractual commitment from the customer's side. Under SALTGRAVE, Ostrey's contract provides one genuine anchor; Marchgate's absence of a contract is the same in both courses, but it is less dangerous when concentrated at 44% than when 62% of the book is simultaneously exposed to a six-month corporate trigger.

**Operational headroom**

At 161/164 tonnes under MORVEDD, there is almost no buffer. A single jig out for unplanned maintenance during a peak dyeing period means Gallowfield fails to deliver against a contract that dedicates two of the four jigs to Thurlmere's sole use. Under SALTGRAVE at 148/164 tonnes, there is slack, a second jig can cover for a first, and the 16 spare tonnes could in principle accommodate a new small customer if Thurlmere does withdraw.

**Capital**

£96K against £180K in cash is 53% of the liquid reserve before any bank draw. The investment is recoverable quickly against the Thurlmere premium, so capital efficiency alone does not settle the question either way. What it does mean is that MORVEDD commits more than half the cash holding to infrastructure whose value is almost entirely dependent on Thurlmere staying. SALTGRAVE retains the full £180K and the bank facility, meaning Gallowfield could respond to future opportunities or absorb a revenue shock without being simultaneously squeezed by a recent capital commitment.

**The Ostrey factor beyond revenue**

Ostrey's 37T at £14.60/kg = £540,200/year. More than the money: twenty-two years of continuous placing represents a relationship that is extremely unlikely to produce a surprise overnight exit, a negotiating ambush, or a parent company's restructuring agenda. Ostrey's offer of a three-year contract at a premium rate is evidence of reciprocal commitment. Gallowfield has no equivalent certainty about Marchgate, a complicated picture about Thurlmere post-Vennerdale, and the Ostrey contract at £14.60 beats the book average. Releasing Ostrey permanently to chase Thurlmere's expansion is trading a known, low-risk, modestly-priced income stream for a high-risk, high-priced stream that is exposed to a corporate trigger outside Gallowfield's control.

**Weighing the decision**

The case for MORVEDD rests almost entirely on the revenue uplift (approximately £285K/year) and the three-year committed headline from Thurlmere. Those are real. But the three-year commitment is not firm; it is three years subject to a six-month change-of-control exit in a contract with a recently-acquired subsidiary of an active acquirer. The probability that Vennerdale makes no further corporate moves affecting Thurlmere across 2027–2029 is not negligible, but it is not high enough to justify placing 62% of the business on that single bet, releasing the most loyal customer on the book, spending over half the liquid reserve, and running at 98% capacity with no operational slack.

SALTGRAVE's lower revenue is a real cost. Turning down £907K of headline committed Thurlmere revenue over three years hurts. But the downside of MORVEDD, if Vennerdale acts, is severe and leaves Gallowfield in a materially worse position than SALTGRAVE's own downside. The asymmetry of outcomes favours the course that preserves Ostrey, protects cash, maintains three-name diversification, and avoids the existential single-point-of-failure at 62%.

CALL
SALTGRAVE

GROUNDS
Thurlmere's six-month change-of-control exit right, held by a recently-acquired Vennerdale subsidiary, combined with the resulting 62% revenue concentration and the permanent loss of a twenty-two-year loyal partner, creates a downside scenario that is potentially existential for Gallowfield, and the forgone revenue premium does not compensate for that structural fragility when Ostrey's contracted three-year commitment provides a far more reliable anchor.
